entry.title: AgentSCM - Catch agent merge conflicts at edit time, not merge time.
entry.summary: Today we're soft-launching the alpha version of AgentSCM for preview and testing. Sub-agents and other team mates contributing to the same source git repo can cause issues not seen until merge or PR time. There are still questions on whether the usual git workflow survives automated agentic coding long-term, but in the interim we are building AgentSCM to build a community of builders looking to work together, as native as possible embedded in their daily workspace(s), to catch conflicts between sub-agents and other contributors' agents in real-time. At the edit: before an agent edits a file, its hook asks a local hub who else holds it. The first overlapping edit isn't applied, and the agent is told who holds the file and their task. It can work elsewhere, ask for a handover, ask you, or repeat the edit, and the repeat always goes through. Before merge: agentscm collisions checks your branches and worktrees and asks git merge-tree which merges would actually conflict. Read-only. No migration: the biggest AI labs are already rethinking source control for agents, which is great to see. You don’t have to make that call yet: keep Git, and two-way Git sync already exists as experimental. Future state: full bi-directional git sync to help you decide when, or if, an agent source code manager should replace your git under scaling pressure. And more workflow tools focused on hundreds or thousands of agent edits, not just human commits/merges/PRs. If you don't want to install but are curious to see it in action: https://agentscm.dev/demo/ To set it up for real: npx agentscm (guided, asks before each change; agentscm uninstall removes it). FAQ Isn't this just worktrees? Won't the agent just retry? What agents work now? Is it a file lock? Telemetry? License? FSL-1.1-ALv2

entry.title: Magnitude vs Ollama: Hardware-Tuned Kernels Cut Inference Latency in Half
entry.summary:
The Problem: Ollama's One-Size-Fits-All Kernel Leaves Performance on the Table
Running a 70B model on heterogeneous hardware exposes Ollama's core architectural constraint: it ships pre-compiled GGML kernels optimized for generic x86/ARM profiles. Your M2 Max, RTX 4090, or AMD 7950X all run the same matrix multiplication routines, ignoring chip-specific SIMD widths, cache hierarchies, and memory bandwidth characteristics. The symptom: identical models produce wildly different time-to-first-token (TTFT) and tokens-per-second across nominally similar hardware configs. Worse, KV-cache thrashing under long contexts (8K+) can degrade throughput by 40% as the static memory allocator fails to adapt to your actual VRAM/RAM split. entry.title: What a call-graph traversal sees that contract-by-contract review cannot
entry.summary: Most smart-contract review reads one contract at a time. You open the file, you look for the usual shapes — reentrancy, unchecked calls, oracle reads — and you write down what you find. The contract is the unit of analysis, and the audit report is a list of findings about that contract. But the largest exploits of the last decade did not happen inside one contract. They happened on a route through several. This post is about building an agent that refuses to certify a contract when its call graph reaches a weakness a real exploit actually used — and what the graph told me that reading contracts one at a time does not.
